rules.title: Massachusetts statewide prohibition on local rent control (G.L. c. 40P)
rules.requirement: No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind. Rent control is defined to include any regulation that in any way requires below-market rents for residential properties. The only exception is for a city or town that accepts chapter 40P, and its regulation must meet three conditions. First, owner compliance becomes entirely voluntary six months after initial adoption. Second, the regulation may not cover occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion or removal of properties from regulation, and may not apply to owners of fewer than ten rental units or to units with a fair market rent above $400. Third, the municipality must compensate owners from general funds for the difference between fair market rent and the controlled rent.
rules.key_value: Local rent control barred statewide. The only exception is voluntary regulation in a municipality that accepts c. 40P: voluntary after 6 months, not for owners of fewer than 10 units or units with fair market rent over $400, and the municipality compensates owners.

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Any regulation under the exception may not apply to a unit owned by a person or entity owning fewer than ten rental units.
coverage.summary: Statewide bar on municipal rent control. The voluntary exception is available only in a city or town that accepts c. 40P, and it excludes units with fair market rent over $400 and small owners (fewer than 10 units).
coverage.owner_conditions: Exception regulation cannot apply to owners of fewer than ten rental units.
coverage.other_conditions: Exception only for a city or town that accepts c. 40P; units with fair market rent above $400 excluded; compliance voluntary after six months.

rules.exemptions: Exception to the ban: a municipality that accepts c. 40P may adopt the limited voluntary regulation described in § 4(a)-(c).
rules.effective_date_note: The documents state no enactment or effective date. Status in_force is inferred from the current official statute text.
rules.quoted_span: No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind, except that any city or town that accepts this chapter may adopt rent control regulation that provides:
rules.review_note: c. 40P does not itself cap rents. It is kept here as the state-local precedence rule for rent control in Massachusetts. No municipal rent control record exists in the inputs: Boston's H.3744 home-rule petition failed. The documents do not say whether any municipality has accepted c. 40P.
rules.source_notes: The definition of rent control and the § 2 'broadly prohibits' language come from the SJC's description in Cella v. Attorney General (DX03). Initiative Petition 25-21 would have struck c. 40P but was barred from the ballot, so c. 40P remains in force. DX14 (secondary) says voters passed the original rent control ban in 1994 but does not tie that date to c. 40P.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: General Laws c. 40P, § 2, "broadly prohibits any regulatory scheme based upon or implementing rent control."

rules.title: Initiative Petition 25-21, An Initiative Petition to Protect Tenants by Limiting Rent Increases (barred from November 2026 ballot)
rules.requirement: The proposed statewide ballot measure would have struck G.L. c. 40P and capped any annual rent increase for 'covered dwelling units' at the lower of the annual CPI increase or five percent. In Cella v. Attorney General (SJC-13893, June 23, 2026), the SJC held the petition relates to religion because it exempts facilities operated solely for religious purposes. Art. 48 therefore bars it from the ballot. The court remanded for a judgment declaring the petition noncompliant and enjoining its placement on the 2026 ballot.
rules.key_value: Proposed cap: lower of annual CPI increase or 5% (never took effect)

rules.title: Bar on discrimination against recipients of public assistance or housing subsidies (G.L. c. 151B, § 4(10))
rules.requirement: It is an unlawful practice for any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against an individual for any of three reasons: because the individual receives federal, state or local public assistance (including medical assistance); because the individual is a tenant receiving housing subsidies (including rental assistance or rental supplements); or because of any requirement of such a program. Landlords may not reject or treat applicants differently because of voucher or assistance status. § 4(7B) separately bars rental advertising that indicates a preference based on public assistance recipiency.
rules.key_value: Source-of-income protection for public assistance and housing subsidy recipients

coverage.summary: Applies to any person furnishing rental accommodations. Subsection 10 states no unit-count, construction-date or owner-occupancy exemption.
coverage.other_conditions: Protects recipients of public assistance and tenants receiving housing subsidies.

rules.effective_date_note: The document does not state when subsection 10 took effect. Status in_force is inferred from the current official statute text.

rules.review_note: The owner-occupied two-family exemption in subsection 7 is not stated for subsection 10. Boston and Cambridge have complementary local source-of-income protections.

rules.title: Fourteen-day notice to quit for nonpayment of rent under a written lease (G.L. c. 186, § 11)
rules.requirement: If a tenant neglects or refuses to pay rent due under a written lease, 14 days' written notice to quit ends the lease. The tenant can defeat termination by paying or tendering all rent due, with interest and costs, on or before the answer date in the possession action. If nonpayment was caused by a government agency's failure or delay in mailing or delivering a subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue the hearing at least 7 days. If all rent, interest and costs are tendered within that time, the court treats the tenancy as not terminated.
rules.key_value: 14 days' written notice; cure through the answer date; at least 7-day continuance for government payment delay

coverage.summary: Tenancies under a written lease where rent is unpaid.

rules.effective_date_note: No effective date stated; current official statute text.
rules.quoted_span: Upon the neglect or refusal to pay the rent due under a written lease, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the lease,
rules.review_note: This is a termination-notice rule, not a list of just causes. The documents show no statewide just-cause or relocation requirement.

rules.title: Notice to determine a tenancy at will (G.L. c. 186, § 12)
rules.requirement: Either party may end a tenancy at will with three months' written notice. If rent is payable at shorter intervals, the notice must equal the interval between payment days or thirty days, whichever is longer. For nonpayment, the landlord may end the tenancy with 14 days' written notice to quit. A tenant who has not received a similar notice in the preceding 12 months can prevent termination by paying the full rent due within 10 days of receipt. Every nonpayment notice must contain the statutory right-to-cure notification. If it is omitted, the cure period extends to the answer date, but the notice otherwise remains valid. If nonpayment was caused by a government payment delay, the court must continue the hearing at least 7 days.
rules.key_value: 3 months' notice (or rent interval/30 days if longer); 14-day nonpayment notice; 10-day cure once per 12 months

rules.title: Reprisal protections for tenants (G.L. c. 186, § 18)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not threaten or take reprisals against a tenant for any of the following: enforcing housing laws through judicial or administrative action, reporting code violations to the board of health or another authority, complaining in writing to the landlord, or organizing or joining a tenants' union. Damages are the greater of 1 to 3 months' rent or actual damages, plus costs and attorney's fees. A rebuttable presumption of reprisal arises if, within six months after the protected activity, the tenant receives any of the following: a notice of termination (except for nonpayment of rent), a rent increase, or a substantial change in tenancy terms. The presumption can be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence of independent justification. Lease waivers are void.
rules.key_value: Damages: 1-3 months' rent or actual damages, plus fees; 6-month presumption of reprisal; rebuttal by clear and convincing evidence

rules.title: Tenant-rights form must accompany a notice to quit for nonpayment (G.L. c. 186, § 31)
rules.requirement: A written notice to quit for nonpayment given to a residential tenant must be accompanied by a state form. The form must include documentation of any repayment agreements and information on rental assistance programs (including RAFT), on summary-process court rules and orders, and on federal or state eviction restrictions. It must prominently state that the notice to quit is not an eviction, that the tenant need not leave immediately, that the tenant is entitled to a legal proceeding, and that only a court order can force the tenant to leave. EOHLC develops the form and publishes it online, with the clause (ii) information in the 5 most common languages besides English. Courts, including the Boston Municipal Court, may not accept a nonpayment summary process filing without proof of delivery of the form.
rules.key_value: State form required with every nonpayment notice to quit; no court filing without proof of delivery

rules.title: Massachusetts security deposit law (G.L. c. 186, § 15B)
rules.requirement:
A security deposit may not exceed the first month's rent. Holding and documentation:
- The deposit must be held in a separate interest-bearing account in a Massachusetts bank.
- A bank receipt is due within 30 days.
- A signed deposit receipt and a statement of condition are due at receipt or within 10 days of the tenancy start, whichever is later.
- Interest of 5% per year, or the lesser rate the bank paid, is payable annually.

Return:
- The deposit or balance must be returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends.
- Deductions are limited to unpaid rent or water charges, unpaid tax-escalation amounts, and reasonable damage beyond wear and tear, supported by a sworn itemized list.

Other duties:
- Records must be kept for 2 years.
- A successor in interest takes over the deposit and must notify the tenant within 45 days.

Penalties: non-compliance forfeits retention rights, and certain violations carry treble damages plus 5% interest, costs and attorney's fees. Waivers are void.

Fee in lieu: as amended effective August 1, 2025, EOHLC regulations may authorize an optional fee in lieu of a deposit. The fee plus any deposit is capped at 1 month's rent in total.
rules.key_value: Max deposit = first month's rent; return within 30 days; 5% interest (or lesser bank rate); treble damages

rules.title: Limit on upfront charges at or before tenancy start, barring landlord application fees (G.L. c. 186, § 15B(1)(b))
rules.requirement:
At or before the start of a tenancy, a lessor or agent of the lessor may not require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay more than the following:
- first full month's rent
- last full month's rent at the same rate
- a security deposit of no more than the first month's rent
- the purchase and installation cost of a key and lock

Any other charge to the lessor or its agent, including an application or screening fee, is therefore not allowed. After the tenancy starts, the lessor may not demand advance rent beyond the current month. No late-rent interest or penalty may be charged until 30 days after rent is due.
rules.key_value: Only first month, last month, deposit (up to 1 month) and lock/key cost may be required upfront; landlord application fees barred; no late penalty until 30 days

rules.title: Broker fee paid only by the party who engaged the broker (G.L. c. 112, § 87DDD½)
rules.requirement: Only a licensed broker or salesperson may be in the business of finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee. A licensed broker or salesperson may contract solely with the prospective tenant or solely with the landlord or landlord's agent. Any fee must be paid only by the party (lessor or tenant) who originally engaged and contracted with the broker or salesperson.
